ety.text: From Old East Slavic икра (ikra), from Proto-Slavic *jьkrā, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ikrā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *yékʷr̥. Compare the semantic development of English roe; however, this is not an etymological cognate.

s.g: a female given name, Ludmila and Lyudmila

ety.text: Probably from Czech Ludmila. Popularized by Russian writers of the early 19th century. May be analyzed as люд (ljud) or лю́ди (ljúdi) + мила́ (milá), short feminine form of ми́лый (mílyj), i.e. dear to the people, beloved by the people.
Borrowed from Arabic مَدْرَسَة f (madrasa, “school”). The pronunciation of this word in many spoken varieties of Arabic has [æ] for underlying /a/, which explains the use of Russian е.
Initialism of министе́рство по чрезвыча́йным ситуа́циям (ministérstvo po črezvyčájnym situácijam).

ety.text: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѧщеньнъ (svęštenĭnŭ). By surface analysis, святи́ть (svjatítʹ) + -енный (-ennyj). Doublet of свячёный (svjačónyj).

ety.text: Desuffixation of the rebracketing of террико́ник (terrikónik) (as террико́н (terrikón) + -ик (-ik)), from French terri conique.

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic щуплъ (ščuplŭ, “weak, pathetic”), from Proto-Slavic *ščuplъ. Cognate with Ukrainian щу́плий (ščúplyj, “skinny, unattractive”), also щупля́вий (ščupljávyj); Belarusian шчу́плы (ščúply, “skinny, unattractive”); Czech štíplý (“lean, slender”); Slovak šťúply (“slender, thin”); Polish szczupły (“thin, lean”). Related to щу́пать (ščúpatʹ, “to feel”); original meaning presumably "so skinny that you can feel the bones".
